articles.title: World Cup 2026: How Michael Olise has become a star that shuns limelight
articles.summary: A footballer who dislikes too much media attention, but Michael Olise might not have much choice if he carries on his World Cup heroics.
articles.body:
Michael Olise is not your typical footballer.

Born and raised in England, he is setting this World Cup alight with France.

The Bayern Munich forward, via Reading and Crystal Palace, usually shuns the spotlight, loves chess, barely celebrates goals and avoids interviews - and does not have a deal with any sportswear or boot companies.

After a season with 25 goals and 28 assists for the Bundesliga champions, the 24-year-old is now seen as one of the world's best players.

Going into Saturday's last-16 tie with Paraguay, Olise has become the first player to assist five goals at one World Cup since Germany's Thomas Hassler in 1994.

Those who have known him since childhood say his reserved nature should not be seen as arrogance - it's just "Michael being Michael".

BBC offers 'Stay Up or Catch Up' for England v Mexico

Why France's Olise is moving into Ballon d'Or picture

United, free and brilliant - can anyone stop France masterclass?

Born in London to a French-Algerian mother, Mina, and a Nigerian father, Vincent, Olise stood out from a young age.

"The sports coaches came to me one day and said have you seen this boy... in year two?" Daniel Coker, Olise's sports teacher at Dr Triplett's CE Primary School in Hayes, London, told BBC Sport.

"When I saw him play...I knew that he was going to be something special."

Coker recalled how Olise - already on Chelsea's books at the time - excelled in every sport he tried.

"At age 10 and 11 that's when I'd get him in everything I could," he added. "He'd come and have a go and just blow us out the water with how good he was."

And already the young Olise did not like any fuss.

"Michael was a quiet and shy boy. He gave so many assists to our team, he'd score loads of goals, but he didn't used to celebrate, he just used to get back straight in and want to go again," said Coker.

"He's not one of those ones to dwell on it and take that moment in. He didn't like the limelight. So when I see that on camera now, when he doesn't celebrate or he runs back, it's just what he's always done."

Headteacher Rachel Anderson remembers it being hard to get Olise back into class after football, particularly if his team hadn't won.

"He would be still kicking the ball around the classroom and it would be like, 'Come on Michael, it's enough now'," she said.

"I think other schools used to sigh and look quite depressed when we turned up with Michael on our team for so many things [different sports] because they knew they didn't stand much of a chance.

"He was a perfectionist and over-analysed everything. He was a bright boy so he did well academically."

It was also at this early age that Olise, who could also have played for England, Nigeria or Algeria, showed signs he would be picking France.

"Rachel said, 'Do you reckon he'll play for England?' I said, I don't know if we'll be lucky enough to have him play for England," Coker added.

"I think Michael really enjoyed that French culture, he went there to visit, he liked learning the language."

But it was not a straightforward path to get there.

Olise's younger brother Richard, 21, is also a professional footballer, although released this summer by Chelsea - just like Michael a decade ago.

Having briefly been at Arsenal, Olise spent seven years with Chelsea's academy before being released aged 14. He then had a short spell at Manchester City, but they too let him go.

Enter Reading, then in the Championship.

However, Brendan Flanagan, the club's head of recruitment, said he had to persuade bosses to recruit the 16-year-old in the summer of 2018.

"Because of the biases that go on in football, it took me a little bit longer to convince people in the building to bring him in because [he was] released from Chelsea, released from Man City - some people would see that as this is going to be a big problem," he told the BBC.

"What might have been deemed as Michael being problematic at other clubs, because he's quiet, he's shy, he's reserved, but we can work with those kids because that doesn't make them a bad kid, it just makes them a little bit different."

But Flanagan was afraid the Royals were going to miss out when Olise's mother said they needed some time to rebuild his confidence after the setbacks.

"She said we're going to do some work with a mentor because he's obviously low in confidence - he's been released from Chelsea, released from Man City - and we just want to make sure that when he comes in to you he's ready for you," added Flanagan.

"I thought to myself, 'That's it, end of - next time I see him he'll be playing against us somewhere'.

"Four weeks later Mina rang me to say right we're ready to go. She was true to her word - that's the kind of people they are, honest genuine people.

"He came in and we never had a single problem with him. He was without a shadow of a doubt the best player that I've ever bought into this building."

Olise was so keen to be on time for training that he would sometimes miss the start of it.

"He would come in at 7 o'clock in the morning for training, that starts at 9, and be asleep in his car when training started," Flanagan said.

Olise made his Reading debut in March, 2019, against Leeds at the age of 17 - days after joining first-team training - and went on to make 73 appearances, scoring seven goals, over three seasons.

It was also there that he got called into the French youth-team set-up.

"It wasn't a surprise that he chose France for me because they were the ones that were first in contact with him," added Flanagan.

"In that 2001 England year group, they generally tended to come from Manchester City, Chelsea, Man Utd, Arsenal, Spurs - not so many from the likes of Reading.

"Michael would be one of those that say, 'Well they chose me first, you didn't want me when I was younger, so that's where I'm going to go'."

Play BBC Sport's World Cup predictor game

How to watch the World Cup on the BBC and ITV

At Reading, Olise had a release clause of £8m which Crystal Palace - managed then by France legend Patrick Vieira - activated in July 2021.

His Premier League quality with the Eagles was evident but initially he was much more of a provider - with 19 assists and six goals in his first two seasons.

In the summer of 2023 Chelsea activated a £35m release clause to re-sign the player they released as a kid.

But to the surprise of nearly everyone, Palace announced Olise had signed a new deal with them instead.

His final season at Selhurst Park was where he really found his shooting boots - netting 10 times, plus six assists, in only 19 games - and 14 starts - in a season disrupted by two different injury spells.

At the end of the 2023-24 campaign, he played for France at the Paris Olympics - under boss Thierry Henry and assistant Gael Clichy.

Former France, Arsenal and Manchester City full-back Clichy told the BBC: "I was really hoping City could actually bring him back, because he was part of the club.

"This is where I actually started to hear about him [at City]. And when he was injury-free at Palace, I started to realise who he was, what kind of player he was.

"I finally met him just before the Olympics and now the world is discovering a player that was always there, but had his own route to get there."

Before the Olympics began, Bayern announced the signing of Olise for about £50m.

Clubs can refuse to let players feature in the Olympics and the German side had done so with his France team-mate Mathys Tel.

But Clichy said Olise told Bayern "he had one wish - to finish the adventure of the Olympics".

"This is really the moment that stood out for us," added Clichy.

"Of course many other moments on the pitch did, but outside of the field a young player who is getting his first big move asking for that was something you don't really see.

"This is the moment we realised that he was a great player, but even more important he was a top man."

Olise helped France reach the Olympic final, where they lost to Spain in extra time.

Olise has kicked on to another level since joining Vincent Kompany's Bayern - and broke into the senior French team almost immediately.

Playing on the right wing, he followed up a campaign with 17 goals and 18 assists with one that saw 25 goals and 28 assists - a total of 88 goal involvements in two seasons.

Former France striker and BBC World Cup pundit Olivier Giroud said: "He's working hard for the team on the pitch, he's got talent but he's a team player.

"He's so relaxed when he's coming inside on his left foot, you know what he's going to do, basically like Arjen Robben back in the day."

Plenty of Olise's viral moments at Bayern include things like trying to stay out of celebrations, avoiding a TV interview and a half-hearted Bundesliga trophy lift.

He likes to walk on to the pitch with sandals before a game to check the surface.

"It's funny to see him walk with the flip-flops on the pitch casually, but this is who he is," said Clichy.

"He's very much a casual guy who has magic in his feet and knows how to express his magic."

Olise's success means he cannot avoid the limelight - and prompted talk of being a potential Ballon d'Or winner.

His chances will improve further if he can help France to glory this summer - he is only one goal off equalling Pele's record of six assists in a World Cup.

"One day Michael could be a contender for the Ballon d'Or," Giroud said.

"If you win trophies, a Ballon d'Or will come, but I think he thinks more collectively than a selfish player, and it's his personality.

"You can see on the pitch, if he can assist, he will assist, even if he could have shot to the goal. So that's what I like. He's a playmaker, but a team player, so it makes him different, special, and he can reach the top of the top."

articles.title: World Cup 2026: Will Nauru, a tiny Pacific island, finally take up football?
articles.summary: Nauru is the only nation to have never played an official international football match and hardly anyone there plays the game. Is that about to change?
articles.body:
Like everywhere, the world's smallest island nation has been gripped by football fever for the past six weeks. But once Spain lifted the World Cup trophy on Sunday, almost every trace of football on Nauru stopped.

Football is almost non-existent on this Pacific island. Nauru has never fielded a team in an official international match and it has just one – hard sand – pitch.

While there is interest in big Premier League matches, and children wear Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo kits, any attempts to actually play football tend to be mocked, unless it's Aussie rules.

But things may be slowly changing as a group of volunteers - led by British former academy player Charlie Pomroy - seek to introduce the game to what was once the world's richest nation per capita but is now heavily reliant on foreign aid and has one of the highest obesity rates in the world.

A social media post from the Nauru Soccer Federation congratulating the new world champions and setting out a dream that "one day we hope to be in Spain's position" may have been fanciful, but the groundwork is real in what it says is the last country not to have had a senior international side.

Laying the foundations, though, on an island where over-mining has left the landscape looking more like a moonscape, has been far from straightforward.

Nauru has tried to develop football previously, but it has never really taken off. The closest it has come to playing an international match was when representative teams faced a Solomon Islands expatriate team in 1994 and a refugee side in 2014.

Its complicated past goes some way to explaining why the world's most popular sport has struggled for participation.

Located in the Pacific Ocean 2,500 miles north east of Australia, Nauru's historical wealth was built on its vast deposits of phosphate from fossilised bird poo.

Nauru, which was a dependent territory of Australia until independence in 1968, was heavily mined in the late 20th Century. The minerals dried up, leaving the country once named Pleasant Island looking ragged, with large parts of its central areas uninhabitable and extremely challenging to farm.

This resulted in most of the 12,000-strong population clustering around the coastal edges with usable space at a premium on an island that measures only 21 square kilometres. And even that is shrinking, with climate change and rising sea levels threatening its very existence.

Its barren land has left the country importing more than 90% of its food – much of which is processed, contributing to 69% of the population being classed as obese and around 40% having type 2 diabetes.

One of its main sources of revenue now is from the Australian immigration detention centre it has housed for much of this century.

Everyday life on the island can be a struggle and sport has been a strong release for many, but the sport of choice is Aussie rules, which 30% of locals play. Also popular are athletics and weightlifting, which Nauru has competed in at the Olympics.

Nauru will host the Micronesian Games in 2028 – a multi-sport event that includes football and will showcase the island's desire to grow its international reputation through sport.

"They are trying to change the image for the better and get involved in more sport," says Pomroy, technical director for Nauru Soccer and one of eight volunteers aiming to develop football on the island.

"They [Nauru] want people to see the country in a more positive light rather than the punchline of a joke.

"So whether it's football, whether it's Aussie rules, whether it's rugby, basketball, cricket, weightlifting... just to be part of building a healthier Nauru is enough.

"But being a football lover, the best way I know how to have an impact is through football."

And the Briton, who is originally from Stevenage and worked at his hometown club when they were still in non-league, has a track history to prove it.

He previously set up a charity in the Cambodian city of Siem Reap which ended up turning into a professional academy that has so far produced 47 players who have progressed to play professionally in the Asian country, and is also running successful programmes in India bringing football to underserved communities.

All of his projects pose different challenges. One of the first challenges in Nauru is getting some footballs on to the island.

The volunteers have launched a campaign to give every child aged four to 14 a ball – roughly 2,000 children – and are working with churches and the island's 11 schools to deliver them. The balls will get delivered 200 at a time by plane to help manage the distribution and avoid potential waste.

Past attempts to introduce football to Nauru have focused on one-off fixtures, including two years ago when former Premier League striker Dave Kitson was appointed to lead a group of 18 Nauruans into a game after a two-week training camp.

Their opponents were set to be a Sunday league team from Reading called XL FC who use football as a way to achieve a healthier lifestyle. That match never happened for financial reasons and so the wait for that inaugural game goes on.

But the ethos has since changed and Nauru Soccer are looking longer term.

"Dave Kitson would have gone, I would have gone, and it would have been great for a couple of months, but it's a lot of money," says Pomroy, who has worked in football in every continent bar South America and Antarctica.

"Let's start a culture on this island of football or sport and help it grow, because it's an important thing. Let's build the ecosystem, not just one-off games.

"My personal dream is that Nauru's first ever international game is played with all kids that are 18 years old that had been coming through our system.

"So, say we found a group of 14-year-olds now and we said, 'Right, let's work with this group over the next three or four years'.

"And by the time they're 17-18 years old, that will be Nauru's first ever national team game."

Once Pomroy arrives for a training camp in December, he will set up coaching programmes for players and aspiring coaches so the sport can continue throughout the year.

A lot of this hinges on being able to find places to play.

Much of the land is privately owned or uninhabitable, but volunteer Tyrone Deiye is hoping to use some of his family's land to create more pitches than the sole one that currently exists - a dusty surface of phosphate over crushed dirt. He also says playing on indoor pitches may be an option.

Pomroy is keen to stress that Nauru Soccer is not trying to "force football down everyone's throat" but says it's about laying a foundation for a sport, promoting healthy lifestyles and building communities.

"The life lessons that you learn through football aren't just on the pitch, not just about winning and losing," says Pomroy, who manages this project while coaching in India.

"It's the friends that you make. It is learning to be humble. It's learning to look after your body. It's learning to get up when you fall down.

"And that's how I've seen it change people across the world. That's the dream for Nauru.

"If we sat here in five years' time, I genuinely believe that we will have a senior team that will be filled with 18, 19, 20-year-olds.

"Then in 20 years' time, someone from Nauru comes up to me and says, 'my life changed through football and the development programme'... That would be the ultimate dream."

Other Pacific island nations play football and expats from these countries sometimes play on Nauru, although Deiye says Nauruans "watch the expats play but they sort of laugh at them because they don't understand the game, they think it's funny".

"A lot of the other Pacific islands have got really good football teams and it makes those guys really happy," adds Deiye, who balances work as an urban planner in Nauru alongside his football work. "Those countries, they're really big into football. I want Nauru to be like that."

Last year, the Marshall Islands played the US Virgin Islands in their first international match. The Pacific island had been the self-proclaimed last nation on earth without a football team, but Nauru have also been claiming this tag.

There was also confusion in the middle of the Covid pandemic when a fake domestic league in Nauru was announced, with the hoax being very detailed down to team names and registered players.

But the Nauru Soccer Federation now has a real website, where it outlines its plans and also sells a national team shirt to raise funds to grow the game. Its main source of money for the project is through fundraisers, but that can be difficult to organise as the volunteers are also balancing full-time work and different time zones.

Even communication between the project's team members can be tricky – sometimes Deiye will not be contactable for a couple of days, only to come back to say that a storm had wiped out the internet on the island.

"This project's not short of challenges, for sure," says Pomroy.

"I think from what I can understand, Nauruans have been promised quite a lot throughout their history and been let down many times.

"So their kind of attitude towards things tends to be 'we believe it when we see it' and they're very reluctant to get their hopes up.

"But in general, the feedback we get is everyone is very, very excited about it."

articles.title: Euro 2016: Inside story of the summer that changed Welsh football
articles.summary: A decade on from Euro 2016, key figures tell BBC Sport Wales the inside story of the summer that changed Welsh football forever.
articles.body:
"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open – his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley – to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there – and that stems from 2016.

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 – a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

articles.title: Carabao Cup 2026-27: When is the third-round draw and which teams are in it?
articles.summary: The third-round draw of the EFL Cup takes place on Wednesday, with nine Premier League teams entering the competition at this stage.
articles.body:
The third-round draw for the 2026-27 Carabao Cup will take place on Wednesday, 26 August following the conclusion of Preston North End vs Everton.

Nine Premier League clubs taking part in European football join the 23 first-round winners from across the English Football League.

Arsenal, Manchester City, Manchester United, Aston Villa, Liverpool, Bournemouth, Sunderland, Brighton and Crystal Palace will enter the competition at this stage, as the top eight Premier League clubs from the 2025-26 season plus Crystal Palace as Conference League winners.

It will be broadcast live on Sky Sports following the conclusion of the third round tie between Preston North End and Everton, kicking off at 20:00 BST that evening.

Nottingham Forest are the only Premier League side guaranteed to not enter the third-round draw after losing their second-round meeting with Leeds United.

Unlike the opening two rounds of the competition, the third round draw is not regionalised.

However, before the match at Deepdale there will be a pre-draw determining which of the Champions League and Europa League clubs will play at home or away in round three.

In order to avoid potential scheduling issues, the eight Champions League and Europa League clubs cannot be drawn against each other in round three.

When the draw takes place, the first eight fixtures decided are the ones involving clubs in the Champions League and Europa League. The remainder of the draw will be an open draw as usual.

Due to clashes with opening weeks of the Champions League and Europa League seasons, the third round will be played across two different weeks. They are the weeks commencing Monday, 7 and Monday, 14 September, 2026.

articles.title: Football Predictions: Play Match of the Day predictor game
articles.summary: Play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game to test your football knowledge and build up your streak.
articles.body:
Fancy testing your football prediction skills?

With the new season under way, BBC Sport has just the thing to keep you entertained every week.

After the success of our World Cup Predictor game, we've rebranded it for the club season as Match of the Day Predictor.

It's simple to play - just predict the outcome of the six fixtures we've selected from across domestic and European competitions every week.

And don't worry if you've joined late - players can join at any time, get involved with the latest round and start building a streak.

Once you've submitted your predictions, you'll also be able to see what others think the outcome of the match will be.

Each round will start on a Friday and the kick-off time of the first match is the deadline to get your predictions in.

Once the round is under way, you've then got the whole week to predict the following set of matches.

The new game also features streaks, so make sure to check in each week to do your predictions.

Every consecutive round you play adds one to your streak, but if you miss a round your streak resets to zero.

Make your selections, or click 'How to Play' to be guided through how it works.

For every match, you either choose a winner or a draw - except for knockout games when only winner options appear.

Once your prediction has been submitted you are unable to change it, so be sure to pick carefully.

After that, wait for the results to roll in and see how you have done.

articles.title: Champions League 2026-27: When is the league phase draw and who is in each pot?
articles.summary: BBC Sport's Ask Me Anything team explains when the league phase draw for the 2026-27 Champions League is, as well as looking at who is in each pot
articles.body:
The league phase draw for the 2026-27 Champions League campaign takes place on Thursday, 27 August at 17:00 BST in Monaco.

A total of 36 teams will enter that stage of the competition and while 29 teams qualified at the end of last season, the remaining seven places are decided by qualifiers that will conclude next week.

In the league phase, each team will face eight different teams once, with four home matches and four away matches.

For the draw, the 36 teams will be placed into four pots with one being the highest-ranked and four being the lowest. The pot placements are based on the club's Uefa club coefficient ranking from the five-season period ending at the conclusion of 2025-26.

Each team will face two teams from each of the four pots and cannot face a team from the same country as themselves.

The teams who finish in the top eight will qualify for the Champions League's round of 16. Those between ninth and 24th will enter the play-off knockout round. The 12 teams ranked between 25th and 36th will exit the competition when the league phase is concluded.

While there are four spots in the league phase of the 2026-27 Champions League yet to be decided, the other 32 teams are confirmed.

We do however know the identities of the teams in each of the four pots.

Premier League clubs Liverpool, Manchester City and Arsenal all feature in pot one alongside back-to-back Champions League winners Paris St-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Inter Milan, Barcelona and Atletico Madrid.

Aston Villa and Manchester United both return to the Champions League this season after not featuring last term. They are in pot two with Borussia Dortmund, Roma, Sporting, Porto, Club Brugge, Real Betis and PSV Eindhoven.

Feyenoord, Lille, Bodo/Glimt, Napoli, RB Leipzig, Villarreal, Shakhtar Donetsk and Galatasaray are all guaranteed to enter the draw in pot three.

The winners of the play-off knockout round match between Fenerbahce and Lyon will also enter pot three.

Slavia Prague, VfB Stuttgart, Lask, Como, Lens and Sabah are all guaranteed to enter in pot four.

The winners of the qualifying ties between Levski Sofia and AEK Athens, Slovan Bratislava and Celje, and Dinamo Zagreb and Viking will follow them into that pot.

articles.title: England Women's U20s World Cup squad named amid boycott threat
articles.summary: Manager Lydia Bedford has named her England squad for the upcoming Fifa U20s Women's World Cup amid ongoing threat of a boycott from European nations.
articles.body:
Manager Lydia Bedford has named her England squad for the upcoming Fifa U20s Women's World Cup amid ongoing threat of a boycott from European nations.

There have been calls for Fifa president Gianni Infantino to resign following the controversy over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

It was aborted after widespread criticism from several confederations, led by Uefa, which has threatened a boycott of all Fifa competitions.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including the World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

The next upcoming Fifa tournament - therefore the first under threat of a boycott - is the U20s Women's World Cup, taking place in Poland from 5 to 27 September.

Speaking to BBC Sport after England had won a warm-up game in Portugal, Bedford spoke for the first time about the potential boycott.

"I was actually at the theatre in London when my dad rang me out of the blue and I was like 'what's happening?' From my perspective the message from leadership all along has been 'just continue as usual' so we have," she said.

"It's not something we've really even spoken to the players about because ultimately every opportunity we have to get on the grass and prepare this team we want to be in the best position possible. So all focus has been on that."

England are one of six nations from Europe taking part in the 24-team tournament alongside France, Italy, Spain, Portugal and hosts Poland.

The young Lionesses have been drawn in Group B with Brazil, Tanzania and Canada, who they face in their opening match on Saturday, 5 September (17:00 BST).

Italy, Portugal and Poland are expected to name their squads next week, while Spain announced theirs on Thursday. France have not confirmed a date.

Bedford has named a 21-player squad to represent England, which includes North Carolina Courage midfielder Erica Meg Parkinson, who received a surprise call-up to the senior squad in March.

"It's an incredibly exciting moment to name the squad and a huge achievement for every player selected," said Bedford.

"We know the level of competition in Poland will be extremely high but we're excited by the prospect of the challenge.

"For the 21 players selected, the focus now is on making the most of this opportunity, representing England with pride, and seeing how far we can go."

articles.title: Where does Man Utd defeat rank among shock opening-game losses?
articles.summary: BBC Sport looks at some of the most shocking Premier League opening-game defeats.
articles.body:
Pre-season optimism can be a dangerous thing, as Manchester United fans have found out the hard way.

On Saturday Michael Carrick's side suffered a shock 2-0 defeat at newly promoted Hull City , who were by far and away the better side.

Hull, back in the Premier League after nine years away, had never previously beaten United in the top flight.

It is the first time United have lost to a newly promoted side on the opening game of the season.

The consolation for United is that it is not the first, nor will it be the last, opening-day upset.

BBC Sport looks at some of the most shocking opening-game defeats.

In 2021, Arsenal were not the Premier League champions they are now, but an opening defeat by Premier League newcomers Brentford was still a major upset.

The Bees were expected to go straight back down to the Championship, but they overpowered Arsenal at a vociferous Gtech Community Stadium.

What a way to mark your first Premier League match, and the first Premier League match without capacity restrictions since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Chelsea fans could not have imagined a worse start to their Premier League title defence.

Gary Cahill's red card 14 minutes in gave Burnley an early man advantage, and Sean Dyche's side led 3-0 by half-time.

Chelsea fought back in the second half, but Sam Vokes has already done the damage at Stamford Bridge.

Cesc Fabregas' late dismissal meant Antonio Conte's side ended the day with nine players.

The Spanish full-back only lasted one season in the Premier League, but he scored Aston Villa 's third to wrap up a superb 3-1 win away at Arsenal .

After scoring 19 goals the previous campaign, Belgian striker Christian Benteke scored twice before Arsenal 's day got even worse when defender Laurent Koscielny was sent off.

This was a bit of a bad-tempered affair - with nine yellow cards and one red. No opening-day game has ever seen so many cards.

2012-13: Queens Park Rangers 0-5 Swansea

Surely nobody has enjoyed a better Premier League debut than Michu?

Swansea's Spanish magician scored twice and set up another as his side thrashed big-spending Queens Park Rangers in West London.

It was a shocking defeat that set the tone of the season for QPR, who despite signing practically a whole new starting XI, ended the season rock bottom of the table.

On the same opening weekend, Brendan Rodgers' tenure as Liverpool boss began with a chastening 3-0 defeat away to West Brom.

Liverpool looked shambolic, summed up by defenders Daniel Agger and Martin Skrtel getting sent off and conceding a penalty respectively.

Romelu Lukaku scored the first of 17 Albion goals during his season on loan from Chelsea .

articles.title: Erling Haaland haircut: Zlatan Ibrahimovic, Jack Grealish & Noel Gallagher shocked
articles.summary: Manchester City striker Erling Haaland reveals his new buzz cut on social media.
articles.body:
Whether it be Zlatan Ibrahimovic, Gareth Bale or Erling Haaland, football has witnessed some iconic man buns over the years.

However, Haaland has decided to begin the new Premier League season with a new - and very different - look.

The Manchester City striker revealed on social media that he had shed his famous blonde locks, posting the caption: "New season, new trim."

Haaland will be hoping his new look brings even more goals as he aims to get off the mark when Enzo Maresca's side face Bournemouth at 14:00 BST on Sunday.

Before cutting his hair, Haaland joked around by showing off some images of his previous hairstyles during his career, and some questionable ideas of how his new hair should look.

Looking nervous as the hairdresser cut the first piece, it didn't take long for Haaland to start smiling about his new appearance.

There were mixed reactions when the 26‑year‑old made video calls to City team-mate Jack Grealish, Oasis' Noel Gallagher and former City manager Pep Guardiola.

Gallagher said: "You look about 17 years old. It's good. Change is good."

Grealish and Guardiola both said they "love" the change.

"You look about 10 years old. That is hilarious. I can't stop looking at the front of your hair. I love it," said Grealish.

"No way. You're lucky you have hair. I would love to have it. I love it," said Guardiola.

Before calling Ibrahimovic, Haaland joked that the former Sweden international told him never to cut his long hair.

"Zlatan told me, never cut your hair, because your strength is in your hair. I'm a bit nervous. I want a buzz cut, like in the military."

It turned out Ibrahimovic was not impressed that Haaland didn't follow his advice.

"What did you do? You lost a bet or what? Block me and erase my number," Ibrahimovic said.

articles.title: Women's Super League: Australians are seen widely in WSL but why not Premier League?
articles.summary: The Premier League used to feature a host of top Australians. Now there is just one player from the country in the competition, but it's a very different story in the WSL.
articles.body:
The Premier League used to feature plenty of Australian talent.

Mark Schwarzer played 514 Premier League games – more than any of his compatriots – while Lucas Neill, Harry Kewell, Brett Emerton, Tim Cahill, Mark Viduka, Mark Bosnich, Mat Ryan, Aaron Mooy and Mile Jedinak all established themselves in England's top flight.

But while there are a number of Australians in the men's Championship, the Premier League has just one representative.

Lucas Herrington, 18, recently joined promoted Hull City from Colorado Rapids in a deal believed to be worth about £17m including add-ons. , external

The picture is very different in the Women's Super League.

There are 13 Australians across eight clubs, including three at Arsenal and three at promoted Charlton Athletic.

So why has England's top women's division become a magnet for Australian players, while the path to the Premier League has become less well-trodden?

Matildas head coach Joe Montemurro suggests one factor is that more men's players are staying in Australia.

So while there are still Australians coming to England to play - such as Portsmouth's Hayden Matthews and Thomas Waddingham, Norwich's Mohamed Toure, Middlesbrough's Riley McGree and Blackburn's Lewis Miller, Montemurro suggests that many more who might have made the long trip are now choosing the A-League instead.

"I think the establishment of the men's professional league in Australia [in 2004] is a reason for a lot of players to stay - they are quite happy to be professionals within their own country," Montemurro told BBC Sport.

"Also, there has been a lot of development in African and Asian countries which has likely widened the net of talent, which means clubs may look elsewhere."

Montemurro thinks the introduction of the WSL second division has probably helped more female Australian footballers play in England.

"The growth of the game in England in club professionalism and with the expansion of WSL to include a second tier [WSL 2] has contributed to more female Australians playing in England," he said.

There are four Australian players in WSL 2 - Alexia Apostolakis (Bristol City), Rachel Lowe (Durham), Kaitlyn Torpey (Newcastle) and Alana Murphy (Nottingham Forest).

Steph Catley, Kyra Cooney-Cross, Caitlin Foord (all Arsenal)

Emily van Egmond, Leah Davidson, Grace Johnston (all Charlton Athletic)

Holly McNamara, Clare Wheeler (both Everton)

Among Australia's men's squad, there are players spread across the world.

Four play in Australia's top flight, two play in the English Championship, three in Japan, and two each in Italy and Germany. The rest feature across countries including Scotland, Austria and the Netherlands.

The table below shows the Socceroos' dispersed overseas pathways.

Low salaries and competitive sporting landscape

The A-League Women (ALW), Australia's top-flight competition, was known as the W-League until 2021. Established in 2008, it initially appeared to be on an upward trajectory - with new clubs, leading Matildas and international players, growing crowds and increased media coverage.

But concerns have since emerged over its financial sustainability.

A 2025 players' union report , external found the ALW was "by far" Australia's lowest-paid professional women's competition. Minimum salaries were A$26,500 (about £13,900), compared with A$74,851 (£39,300) in women's cricket and A$67,337 (£35,400) in the AFL - the Australian rules competition.

The A-League Men and ALW are also the only major Australian sports competitions without a collective bargaining agreement, leaving the domestic game exposed to the threat of industrial action.

With average WSL salaries reported at about £47,000 in 2022 , the financial gap may well be a factor in why more female Australian players are choosing England.

Chelsea and Australia international Ellie Carpenter recently criticised , external the state of the Australian women's game after a pre-season friendly against Sydney FC.

"It's disappointing to see where the league is at here now in Australia, especially coming off the back of the World Cup in 2023 and the buzz here," Carpenter said.

"I really think that we need to follow that and we need to invest more."

Asked if she might return to play in Australia, Carpenter said finances would be a barrier.

"I don't think that's really on the cards, financially, for me to come back here," Carpenter said.

"Hopefully that changes and ending my career in Australia will be possible."

In 2025, Football Australia reported 1.93 million Australian participants , external , making it the country's most-played sport. Yet despite the Socceroos qualifying for six successive men's World Cups, Australia has no dedicated national headquarters for its teams, coaching programmes and administration.

The Home of the Matildas facility in Melbourne opened in 2023 but is not a permanent base for both senior national teams. The Socceroos continue to train at different venues depending on fixtures and availability.

That contrasts with nations such as England and France, which have dedicated centres at St George's Park and Clairefontaine.

Former Socceroos coach Graham Arnold described Football Australia as " homeless , external " in 2024 after his side prepared for World Cup qualifiers against Lebanon at the NSW Rugby League Centre of Excellence.

Montemurro believes Australia's size means more than one centre may be needed.

"We probably need one or two and we need some geographical touch points where we maybe have one where all the northern states can meet and then all the southern states can meet accordingly," he says.

"I think it would be important to have a couple of national centres where we can reconvene a lot of our development squads and our youth squads on a more regular basis.

"I believe a couple of base hubs in Australia could help our youth development."

Australia co-hosted the Women's World Cup in 2023, with the Matildas reaching the semi-finals for the first time after they beat France.

Their rise since then has turned them into one of Australia's most recognisable sporting brands, opening the door to opportunities overseas - evidence of the lasting impact that hosting a major tournament can have.

"The Women's World Cup in 2023 changed perception of the football landscape, not just the perception of the players but also the level of coaches, administrators and the general perception of football in Australia," Montemurro says.

articles.title: Derek McInnes: Rangers manager could be in stand for first Old Firm game after hearing date set
articles.summary: Derek McInnes could be in the stand for his first Old Firm match as Rangers manager after a hearing date of 31 August was set for his appeal against a touchline ban.
articles.body:
Derek McInnes could be in the stand for his first Old Firm match as Rangers manager after a hearing date of 31 August was set for his appeal against a four-match touchline ban, one game of which is suspended.

The penalty issued in July related to McInnes' spell as Hearts boss last season, when he described the decision to award Celtic a late penalty at Motherwell in May as "disgusting".

A stoppage-time spot-kick for handball was converted by Kelechi Iheanacho and Celtic's 3-2 victory at Fir Park on 13 May kept them one point behind Hearts, who they beat to the title a few days later in a final-day decider.

Rangers argued the remarks were "directed at the decision, rather than representing any broader criticism of officials" when announcing their intention to contest the ban.

And McInnes, who could be in the stand for games against Falkirk, Motherwell and Celtic, added: "I don't agree with it and the club don't agree with it. I'm glad that we're going to appeal against that.

"I've been a manager for 19 years and you know you're going to be asked about contentious decisions and all the rest of it.

"I've never wanted to make it personal. For me, the decision was wrong. I feel as though I made my points at the hearing.

"Broadcasters pay a lot of money to hear managers' reactions. We've got to be careful that we don't have managers and players who have to be really sure of themselves and check themselves before answering a question.

"At no point was I wanting to inflame a situation. The situation was already being discussed before I did my Press. It was quite a big moment in the season and there was a lot of emotion, but I felt as though what I said was controlled."

The games against Falkirk away on 2 September and Motherwell three days later at home immediately after the hearing are in the Scottish Premiership, while the 13 September visit of Celtic is in the quarter-finals of the League Cup.

Girona winger Kim to undergo Rangers medical

Visit our Rangers page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

Speaking to Sky Sports after a win against Falkirk at Tynecastle on the same night as Celtic's win at Fir Park, McInnes said: "When you heard Celtic got a 96th-minute penalty that was going to VAR and they were checking it, you just assume what's happened is they get the penalty.

"Having seen it again, it's disgusting. It is. I don't think it's a penalty kick.

"But we're up against it. We're up against everybody."

Scottish FA head of referees Willie Collum later backed the call, citing "clear evidence" of Motherwell's Sam Nicholson's hand and arm "in an unnatural position" - and the resulting contact "a punishable handball".

Referee John Beaton's contact details were posted online, with police keeping his home under surveillance. A teenager was then charged "in connection with a data protection offence".

The statement from Rangers added: "Respect for officials and legitimate scrutiny are not competing principles.

"Managers, players and clubs must be able to speak honestly about major decisions if Scottish football is serious about raising standards and maintaining trust.

"Scrutiny, transparency and accountability should be seen as part of improving standards, not as a threat to them."

articles.title: Tony Docherty is new Scotland Under-21 head coach, assisted by Steven Naismith
articles.summary: Tony Docherty is named Scotland Under-21 head coach, with Steven Naismith as assistant.
articles.body:
Tony Docherty has been named Scotland Under-21 head coach, with Steven Naismith as assistant.

Former Dundee and Ross County manager Docherty, 55, previously worked as part of Gordon Strachan's Scotland backroom team and ex-Hearts boss Naismith, 39, was assistant to Steve Clarke for almost a year.

Clarke left the national team job following Scotland's World Cup campaign, with Sebastien Pocognoli recently announced as his successor.

Docherty, who assisted Derek McInnes at Aberdeen and Kilmarnock, replaces Scot Gemmill, who had been in the position for almost a decade.

"I am looking forward to getting straight to work and I'm delighted I'll be joined by Steven, who I have so much respect for as a coach, as a player, and as an individual," said Docherty.

"I had several lengthy conversations with [Scottish FA chief football officer] Craig Mulholland and then met Sebastien Pocognoli as part of the process. Everyone is aligned on creating a clear national team and player identity and about doing everything we can to improve every aspect of the national game.

"I'm equally enthused by the challenge of supporting our clubs, in a unique new initiative, ensuring we all work together creating real growth.

"It's up to us to make sure the national team experience is the best that it can be, while pushing young Scottish players to be the best they can be."

Youthful Pocognoli the brave choice for Scotland job

Pocognoli 'feels connection' with 'passionate' Scotland

Naismith added: "Representing Scotland, in various capacities now, has meant so much to me.

"I've learned a lot along the way and it's great to have the opportunity, alongside Tony and the rest of the staff, to pass those experiences on to those hoping to carve out international careers.

"I was fortunate to be part of the staff that took Scotland back to the World Cup for the first time in 28 years and there is a burning desire within the Scottish FA to ensure there is no repeat of that wait.

"There are strong foundations to build on, but there is an obvious drive, energy and focus to enhance every aspect further and see how far it can take us.

"I am delighted to, of course, be coaching a Scotland team with Tony, but I am most excited by the mentorship programme I will lead, sharing my experiences as a player, manager and coach with some of our brightest young players."

articles.title: Cole Palmer & Morgan Rogers shine in Chelsea win but Robert Sanchez struggles
articles.summary: While Chelsea's front three produced a sparkling display in their win over Fulham, goalkeeper Robert Sanchez remains a major concern.
articles.body:
If football is won in both boxes, it seems as though Chelsea have one far better covered than the other.

Xabi Alonso began his Stamford Bridge reign with an entertaining 3-2 Premier League win at west London rivals Fulham on Monday - and their new-look front three stole the show.

Morgan Rogers, making his debut after his club record £117m summer move from Aston Villa , combined with Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro to produce a devastating attacking display.

All three scored, with Palmer in particular looking back to his best after a difficult year hampered by injuries, culminating in his omission from England's World Cup squad.

At the other end, though, questions remain over goalkeeper Robert Sanchez after two errors contributed to Fulham 's goals from Josh King and Gonzalo Garcia.

Alonso said his front three needed to "lead the rest" so that the "other ones will follow".

But Sanchez has some catching up to do - and when asked about his mistakes, Alonso could only stress the collective responsibility of the team.

"We need to accept and learn from them [the mistakes]," said the Spaniard. "This is going to be a process.

"All the lines, from the strikers, the midfielders, the defence, the goalkeepers, we want to do better in everything."

After the match, ex- Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher - a former team-mate of Alonso - said on Sky Sports that Palmer, Rogers and Joao Pedro are "as good as anything in the Premier League right now".

He also said they would "never win the league with Sanchez in goal".

Palmer shines as Alonso begins Chelsea reign with win at Fulham

Rogers & Palmer star but Sanchez struggles - Fulham v Chelsea player ratings

It took Joao Pedro just 31 seconds to open the scoring, latching on to a pass from Palmer and lifting his shot over Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno for Chelsea 's fastest goal since October 2016.

After King equalised, Rogers marked his debut with a goal before half-time by tapping in from close range.

But it was Palmer - scorer of Chelsea 's third - who stood out most.

He has endured a frustrating 18 months since a niggling groin problem disrupted his sensational start to life at Stamford Bridge, highlighted by the fact he matched last season's Premier League assist tally by setting up Joao Pedro.

His trickery and creativity was on display throughout against Fulham , along with an impressive work-rate. This was more like the Palmer we saw during his first season at Stamford Bridge - and like the one who tore Paris St-Germain apart during last year's Club World Cup final.

"Over the summer I rested, I recharged and, yeah, I'm ready and I'm hungry," Palmer, who is now just two goals away from 50 in the Premier League, told Sky Sports.

During Chelsea 's pre-season tour of Australia, he spoke of having a point to prove and admitted a lengthy summer break felt unusual after featuring in major tournaments in each of the previous three years.

"Cole Palmer was sensational," said former Manchester United defender Gary Neville on Sky Sports. "Him and Morgan Rogers were electric with Joao Pedro - the front three were brilliant.

"That tonight was the old Cole Palmer. It was unbelievable to watch. One of the best things I've seen this weekend."

How two best mates and Joao Pedro linked up

While Palmer and Joao Pedro have generally carried Chelsea 's biggest attacking threat in recent times, they have now been joined by the impressive Rogers.

His arrival reunites him with Palmer, an ex- Manchester City team-mate and someone he described after the win at Craven Cottage as his "best friend in football".

"He had a difficult season with injuries and stuff last year - and you could see it in his eyes in pre-season and training that he's ready this year and ready to prove people wrong," said Rogers when asked about Palmer's display.

"You saw that with that performance. He was the best player on the pitch by a mile and that's what he does. It's good to have him on our side."

Indeed, it was also encouraging how Rogers, whose pre-season was shortened by his involvement in England's run to third place at the World Cup, looked so fit and powerful.

Rogers is the first Chelsea player to score on his Premier League debut since Christopher Nkunku in 2023 - and the first to create five chances in his first league appearance since records began in 2003-04.

This was also the first time Chelsea supporters sang the new Rogers chant in the away end.

Like Palmer, Joao Pedro missed out on the World Cup - as a high-profile omission from Brazil's squad - but returned in pre-season with eight goals in seven games.

It was no surprise to see him on the scoresheet so early in the Premier League campaign, having inherited the number nine shirt from Liam Delap, who was left out of the squad on Monday, and following the contract extension the Brazilian signed at the weekend.

"Great combination, great quality," Alonso told BBC Match of the Day when asked about his front three.

"We know if we reach them [Joao Pedro, Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer] in good positions, they have this talent to create special things and I am very happy the three forwards have scored.

"We need to put them in the best situations. I am happy for the three of them. They played for the team."

'Sanchez will undermine everything they do'

Yet questions remain over Sanchez, who allowed King's low strike to go straight through him for Fulham 's equaliser and then tamely parried Timothy Castagne's shot into a dangerous area for Garcia to head in from close range to set up a nervy finish.

"They have strengthened in every position of the pitch but you cannot take a chance on goalkeepers," said Neville.

"I've said before it's the most difficult position on the pitch, it's the one that carries the most scrutiny and if you have got a goalkeeper who's making mistakes and is anxious, it will undermine everything you're trying to do.

"It's a problem. You've got to say it's a problem."

King's equaliser in the 23rd minute had an expected goals on target (xGoT) value of just 0.05, making it the lowest-rated shot to result in a goal during the opening weekend of the Premier League season.

In other words, Sanchez really should have saved it.

He did make a number of other saves, but he also conceded a corner after failing to clear the ball before it ran out of play and was later unconvincing when coming off his line to deal with a long ball, with Antonee Robinson missing the target to let him off the hook.

While Alonso defended his goalkeeper after the game, in his pre-match news conference on Thursday he had said: "The pitch is the boss of everything. I don't decide. The players need to show me."

That message applied to his goalkeepers - Sanchez and number two Mike Penders, 21, who is waiting to make his debut after returning from a successful loan spell at Strasbourg.

With the transfer window still open, many Chelsea fans will be asking whether the club need a new first-choice goalkeeper.

As Carragher said: "They have to sort the goalkeeping issue out because it's going to come back and haunt them again this season as it did tonight."

articles.title: Troy Deeney's Team of the Week: Trafford, Mendy, Guehi, Palmer, Pedro
articles.summary: After every round of Premier League matches this season, Troy Deeney gives us his team of the week. Do you agree with his choices?
articles.body:
After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

James Trafford ( Leeds ): It's been a big-pressure move for Trafford going to Leeds . I think at the World Cup with England he thought, 'I should be playing more' and he obviously didn't get the time and needed a move away. He produced a strong performance for Leeds at Nottingham Forest and was one of the few goalkeepers to keep a clean sheet.

Keane Lewis-Potter ( Brentford ) : He was excellent defensively and attacking wise and got his goal. He is one of Brentford 's underrated players and sort of sums up their team. Nobody speaks about him or Brentford but they hammered Tottenham .

Nobel Mendy ( Hull City ) : He was so good and powerful. He offered so much defensively to Hull and scored their second goal. He was a real powerhouse. Hull will definitely need him and he is one of those defenders where you think, 'I don't want to play against him'.

Maxence Lacroix ( Chelsea ) : Lacroix just added a level of experience and calmness to Chelsea and also got an assist. He read the game and understood what was needed and provided the maturity that will add so much to Chelsea going forward. It was a very good debut for the France defender.

Maxim de Cuyper ( Brighton ) : He scored, had an assist and was excellent for Brighton . Opponents Aston Villa were poor, but if you watched the first 20 minutes you would see he was really aggressive and really set the tone with the pressure.

Marc Guehi (Man City) : I'll have Guehi in as my holding midfielder. He should have scored two against Bournemouth because he missed a massive chance before he ended up scoring. But he got the equaliser and offered a lot more of a calming presence than City's £116m record signing Elliot Anderson - Guehi controlled the game a little bit more.

Vitaly Janelt ( Brentford ): He is one of those big, powerful and dominant players who does the basics really well. He mixed that with a goal against Spurs and you don't really speak about him, but he was always the one breaking up play and doing the horrible things really well.

Christos Tzolis ( Arsenal ) : A lot of people are talking about Arsenal and how they're great. That is absolutely true. And so is the bit of business they did bringing this young man in from Club Brugge. So many goals and assists he brings to the team, but also a calming influence and tenacity as well. Look at Gabriel Martinelli, Leandro Trossard, he feels to me like both of them in one. He has a lot more output than those guys. He's going to be a beast for this year.

Anthony Elanga ( Newcastle ): Last season I though he was treated poorly by Eddie Howe because he was one that kept being put on the bench, being introduced late or would be the first one to come off. But he showed in a new formation, under a new manager and somebody who believes in him that he can use his pace and power. As a result he looks like a completely different player and he looked happy. He ran past Milos Kerkez like he wasn't there despite the Liverpool left-back having a five-yard start and produced an unbelievable finish for his goal.

Cole Palmer ( Chelsea ) : One we were all talking about, and should've gone to the World Cup with England. Feels like he's got a point to prove, feels like he's been working hard. The injuries from last year skewed everyone's vision. Everything he did at Fulham was positive. Ran forward with pace, looked like he could move. He had those issues with the groin but now he's chopping and turning.

Joao Pedro ( Chelsea ) : My old Watford team-mate and someone who will make everyone question when they said he wasn't good enough. He's going to have a breakout year.

Sergej Jakirovic ( Hull City ) : Tactically brilliant and had a gameplan for Manchester United . His side gave a bit of space away but wouldn't get transitioned on, gave away a lot of cheap fouls. Went forward in the wide areas, crossed it and finished the action. He was very impressive in the Championship last year, spoke well but never got too high or too low. He'll take a few by surprise but I'm concerned they won't have the quality in the team. For now, who cares?

articles.title: PFA Awards: Sir Kenny Dalglish and Karen Carney win merit awards
articles.summary: Liverpool and Scotland legend Sir Kenny Dalglish and Lionesses great Karen Carney win the Professional Footballers' Association's merit awards for 2026.
articles.body:
Sir Kenny Dalglish and Karen Carney have won the Professional Footballers' Association's merit awards for 2026.

The awards honour individuals who have made a lasting contribution to football.

The PFA Awards ceremony will be held in Manchester on Tuesday evening, where the men's and women's players' player of the year winners will be announced.

Dalglish enjoyed a prolific career as both player and manager, becoming Scotland's most-capped men's international with 102 appearances and matching Denis Law's national team record of 30 goals.

At club level, he began with a trophy-laden spell at Celtic before moving to Liverpool for a British record fee in 1977 and becoming an integral part of the club's golden era.

Over the next 14 years, Dalglish won eight First Division titles and three European Cups across 515 appearances for Liverpool and was runner-up for the Ballon d'Or in 1983.

Appointed player-manager in 1985, he guided the club to three league titles and two FA Cups - including the Double in 1985-86 - before retiring from playing in 1990.

After resigning as Liverpool's manager in February 1991, Dalglish led Blackburn to the Premier League title in 1995 and had stints with Celtic, Newcastle and Liverpool again, where he won the 2012 League Cup.

Off the field, Dalglish remains a significant figure in Merseyside. He led the club through the aftermath of the Hillsborough disaster in 1989, earning praise for his support of the bereaved families, and has raised millions of pounds to support cancer care and treatment through the Marina Dalglish Appeal, set up in 2005 following his wife's treatment for breast cancer.

Dalglish, 75, announced in June 2026 that he is having treatment for cancer.

Former England attacking midfielder Carney was a member of the Arsenal side that completed a historic quadruple in 2006-07 - winning the league, FA Cup, League Cup and Uefa Women's Cup, the forerunner to the Women's Champions League.

She spent two seasons with Chicago Red Stars before returning in 2011 to home club Birmingham City, where she had started her career. Carney scored an extra-time equaliser as Birmingham won the FA Cup the following season.

Moving to Chelsea in late 2015, Carney won the WSL and FA Cup double in 2017-18 and later served as club captain before ending her playing career in 2019.

On the international stage, Carney made her England debut as a 17-year-old in 2005. She went on to score 32 goals in 144 appearances for the Lionesses and helped England finish third at the 2015 Women's World Cup.

That was one of eight major tournaments for Carney with England, while she also represented Great Britain at the 2012 Olympics.

Since retiring, Carney, 39, has built a career as a broadcaster and analyst and was appointed by the UK Government to chair an independent review, published in 2023, into the future of domestic women's football.

articles.title: Abdul Abdulmalik: £1.5m-rated National League star asks to leave Boreham Wood
articles.summary: Boreham Wood forward Abdul Abdulmalik says he is "capable of reaching the top" after the National League side reject a £1.5m offer from Swedish club Djurgarden.
articles.body:
Boreham Wood forward Abdul Abdulmalik said he is "capable of reaching the top" after the National League side rejected a £1.5m offer from Swedish club Djurgarden.

The 23-year-old has been the subject of serious interest from the Swedish top-flight side, who had an offer of £1m rejected earlier this month.

Boreham Wood do not want to sell Abdulmalik, with manager Luke Garrard saying "he is our player" after the forward was left out of the London club's 3-0 victory over Forest Green on Saturday.

"Everyone at Boreham Wood FC and the incredible fans have played a massive part [in my journey]. You will always have my respect," Adbulmalik said in a statement released by his agent.

"With this said, I'm ready for the next challenge. I'm ready to prove to myself and those around me that I'm capable of reaching the top."

Abdulmalik enjoyed a breakout season in 2025-26, scoring 17 goals and providing 10 assists as Boreham Wood reached the National League play-off final, where he scored and assisted at Wembley.

Djurgarden's £1.5m offer would have broken the record fee paid for a fifth-tier player in England, set in 2012 when Leicester paid Fleetwood Town £1m for Jamie Vardy.

"Through sheer hard work and perseverance, the opportunity to progress has come around. This is my chance to push myself as a footballer, elevate my game and most importantly fulfil my promise to the ones around me," Abdulmalik continued.

"Opportunities like this are rare, especially within the National League where some of the hardest working talent is overlooked.

"The game of football is forever changing and decisions are fast paced. There's no guarantee that the same chances come knocking twice.

"I owe it to myself and the kids growing up just like me to fight for this one I've been offered."

Abdulmalik came through Millwall's academy, progressing through the club's youth system and representing England at under-17 level.

He was part of the club's Under-21s successes - securing consecutive Professional Development League South titles in 2022-23 and 2023-24.

However, a pathway into consistent first-team football did not materialise and Abdulmalik was released in 2024, before Boreham Wood signed him as a free agent.

BBC Sport has contacted Boreham Wood for comment.
